essays.stem: Describe how to make a white chicken stock, from preparing the bones to storing the stock.
essays.modelAnswer: I use raw chicken bones and carcasses, kept in the fridge until I need them. I chop them into pieces and remove any fat. To keep the stock clear, I blanch them: I cover them with cold water, bring them to the boil, then drain and rinse them. I put the bones in a clean stockpot and cover them with fresh cold water. I bring it slowly to a simmer and skim off the scum and fat that rise. I add a mirepoix of onion, carrot and celery, cut into large pieces, and a bouquet garni of thyme, bay leaf and parsley stalks, with a few peppercorns. I do not add salt, because the stock may be reduced later. I let it simmer very gently for about 2–3 hours, skimming often, without stirring or boiling hard, which would make it cloudy. Then I strain it through a fine strainer or muslin. I cool it quickly in shallow containers in an ice bath, remove the fat from the top, cover and label it with the name and date, and keep it in the fridge at 5 °C or below.
markingPoints: Bones prepared and blanched (boiled, drained, rinsed) for a clear white stock
Cold water start, brought slowly to a simmer and skimmed
Mirepoix, bouquet garni and peppercorns; no salt (reason)
Gentle simmer for about 2–3 hours, skimming; no hard boiling
Strain finely; cool quickly; label, date and refrigerate at 5 °C or below

essays.stem: Compare white stock, brown stock and fish stock. Say how each is made and what each is used for.
essays.modelAnswer: A white stock is made from raw chicken or veal bones that are blanched, not browned, then simmered with onion, carrot, celery and herbs for about 2–3 hours for chicken. It is pale and clear and is used for white sauces such as velouté, cream soups, chicken soup and rice dishes. A brown stock is made from beef or other bones that are roasted in a hot oven until brown, with the mirepoix browned too, and often a little tomato paste. The bones are covered with cold water and simmered for many hours, often 6–8, skimming often. It is dark brown and rich and is used for brown sauces such as espagnole and gravy, stews and brown soups. A fish stock is made from the bones and heads of white fish, washed well, with the gills removed, and gently sweated with onion and herbs before cold water is added. It is simmered for only about 20 minutes, because longer cooking makes it bitter and cloudy. It is used for fish sauces, fish soups and seafood dishes.
markingPoints: White stock: blanched, not browned, bones; about 2–3 hours for chicken
White stock uses: velouté, cream soups, chicken dishes
Brown stock: roasted bones and vegetables, long simmer; used for brown sauces, gravy, stews
Fish stock: white fish bones, gills removed, about 20 minutes only (reason: bitter)
Fish stock uses: fish sauces and soups

essays.stem: Describe how to make a béchamel sauce, and one sauce made from it.
essays.modelAnswer: For about 1 litre of béchamel, I use about 100 g butter, 100 g plain flour and 1 litre of milk, or the amounts in the Centre's recipe. I warm the milk in a pan with an onion studded with a clove and a bay leaf, to add flavour. In a heavy pan, I melt the butter on a low heat, add the flour and stir with a wooden spoon for a few minutes to make a white roux, without letting it colour. I take the pan off the heat and let it cool a little. I add the warm milk a little at a time, stirring well each time so that no lumps form. When all the milk is in, I bring the sauce slowly to the boil, stirring all the time, and simmer it gently for about 10 minutes to cook the flour. I season it with salt and white pepper and strain it if needed. To make a cheese (Mornay) sauce, I take the béchamel off the heat and stir in grated cheese, and sometimes an egg yolk, until it melts. I use it for macaroni pie or over cauliflower.
markingPoints: Correct ingredients and rough proportions (equal fat and flour to milk)
Infuse the milk with onion, clove and bay leaf
Make a white roux without colour
Add milk gradually, stirring; boil and simmer to cook out the flour; season
A correct derivative, e.g. cheese (Mornay) sauce, and its use

essays.stem: Name the five classical mother sauces, and say what each is made from.
essays.modelAnswer: The mother sauces are the basic sauces from which many other sauces are made. The first is béchamel, a white sauce made from milk thickened with a white roux of butter and flour, often flavoured with onion and bay leaf. The second is velouté, made from a white stock, such as chicken or fish stock, thickened with a blond roux, which is cooked a little longer than a white roux. The third is espagnole, a brown sauce made from brown stock, a brown roux, browned mirepoix and tomato, simmered for a long time; it is reduced with more brown stock to make demi-glace. The fourth is tomato sauce, made from tomatoes cooked with onion, carrot, garlic, herbs and stock, then blended or strained. The fifth is hollandaise, a warm emulsion sauce made by whisking egg yolks with a reduction of vinegar and peppercorns, then whisking in melted or clarified butter. From these come sauces such as cheese sauce, mushroom sauce and gravy.
markingPoints: Béchamel: milk and white roux
Velouté: white stock and blond roux
Espagnole: brown stock, brown roux, mirepoix and tomato
Tomato sauce: tomatoes, vegetables, herbs and stock
Hollandaise: egg yolks emulsified with butter (and an acid reduction)

essays.stem: Describe four ways of thickening sauces and soups, and say how each is used.
essays.modelAnswer: The first way is a roux, which is equal amounts of fat and flour cooked together. Liquid is added a little at a time and stirred, then the sauce is simmered to cook the flour, as in béchamel. The second is a starch mixed with a little cold liquid, such as cornflour or arrowroot. The paste is stirred into the hot liquid near the end and brought back to the boil until it thickens, which is quick and good for clear, glossy sauces. The third is beurre manié, which is butter and flour kneaded together. Small pieces are whisked into a simmering sauce or stew at the end to thicken it. The fourth is a liaison of egg yolks and cream, which is mixed with a little of the hot soup, then stirred in off the boil and not boiled again, or it will curdle. Soups can also be thickened by blending in cooked vegetables or pulses, such as pumpkin, yam or red peas, as in Jamaican soups, and sauces can be thickened by reduction, boiling them so water steams off.
markingPoints: Roux: fat and flour, liquid added gradually, simmered to cook the flour
Starch slurry (cornflour or arrowroot) mixed with cold liquid first
Beurre manié whisked in at the end
Liaison of yolks and cream added off the boil; not reboiled
Vegetable or pulse purée, or reduction (e.g. pumpkin or yam in Jamaican soups)

essays.stem: Describe how to make hollandaise sauce, and explain how to keep it safely during service.
essays.modelAnswer: I melt or clarify the butter and keep it warm. I make a reduction by boiling a little vinegar with crushed peppercorns until only a spoonful is left, then cool it with a little cold water. I put the yolks (pasteurised, if the Centre's food safety plan says so) and the reduction in a bowl over a pan of barely simmering water, not touching the water, and whisk until the mixture is thick, pale and creamy, like a ribbon. I take it off the heat and slowly whisk in the warm butter, a little at a time, so the emulsion forms and does not split. I season it with salt and a little lemon juice. If it starts to split, I whisk it slowly into a fresh yolk or a spoon of warm water. Hollandaise is kept warm, not hot, so it does not split, but this is not hot enough to stop bacteria growing. So I make it in small batches, close to service, keep it covered in a warm place, and throw away what is left after the time the Centre's food safety plan allows. It is never kept for the next day.
markingPoints: Warm melted or clarified butter and a vinegar and peppercorn reduction
Yolks and reduction whisked over barely simmering water until thick (pasteurised yolks if the plan says)
Butter whisked in slowly to form the emulsion; seasoned with lemon and salt
A split sauce saved with a fresh yolk or warm water
Food safety: small batches, kept warm for a short time only, leftovers thrown away

essays.stem: Describe how to make Jamaican red peas soup with spinners.
essays.modelAnswer: The night before, I pick over the dried red peas (kidney beans), wash them and soak them in cold water. I also soak any salted meat, such as pigs' tail or salt beef, to remove extra salt. Next day, I throw away the soaking water, put the peas and meat in a large pot with fresh water, and boil them hard first, because raw kidney beans contain a natural toxin that boiling destroys. Then I simmer them, skimming the scum, until the peas are soft, which can take 1–2 hours, or less in a pressure cooker used as the maker says. I add diced yam, coco and carrot, crushed garlic, onion, scallion, thyme, pimento berries and a whole Scotch bonnet pepper, which must not burst. To make spinners, I mix flour, a pinch of salt and water into a firm dough, and roll small pieces between my palms into long, thin dumplings. I add them to the soup and simmer until they are cooked and the yam is tender. Some peas break down and thicken the soup. I take out the pepper and thyme stalks, taste with a clean spoon, adjust the seasoning, and serve it hot.
markingPoints: Soak the peas (and salted meat) overnight; throw away the soaking water
Boil hard in fresh water first (safety reason), then simmer until soft, skimming
Add ground provisions and seasonings, with a whole unburst Scotch bonnet
Spinners: firm flour dough rolled into long thin dumplings, added and cooked
Remove the pepper and thyme stalks, taste with a clean spoon, serve hot

essays.stem: Describe how to make a cream of pumpkin soup, including how to blend it safely.
essays.modelAnswer: I peel the pumpkin, remove the seeds and cut it into even pieces. I chop onion, garlic and a little carrot. In a heavy pot, I sweat the onion and garlic in butter or oil on a low heat, without colour, until soft. I add the pumpkin and carrot, a sprig of thyme and enough vegetable or chicken stock to cover. I bring it to the boil, then simmer until the pumpkin is very soft, about 20–30 minutes. To blend it safely, I let the soup cool a little first. If I use a jug blender, I fill it only part way, fit the lid firmly, hold it down with a folded cloth, and start on a low speed, so hot soup cannot spray out. A stick blender is used with the head kept under the surface, and it is switched off before it is lifted out. I return the soup to the pot, add cream or coconut milk, and reheat it gently without boiling hard. I check the thickness, taste with a clean spoon and season. I serve it hot in warm bowls, with a swirl of cream and chopped herbs or croutons.
markingPoints: Prepare the pumpkin and vegetables evenly; sweat the onion without colour
Add stock and simmer until the pumpkin is very soft
Blend safely: cool slightly, part-fill, lid on with a cloth, start on low (or stick blender kept under the surface)
Finish with cream or coconut milk, reheat gently, check thickness and seasoning
Serve hot in warm bowls with a suitable garnish

essays.topic: Food safety: cooling, storing and reheating
essays.stem: Explain how to cool, store and reheat stocks, sauces and soups safely.
essays.modelAnswer: Stocks, sauces and soups are moist and full of nutrients, so bacteria grow fast in them in the danger zone, between 5 °C and 63 °C. A large pot cools slowly, so I never leave it out to cool. I strain or portion the food into shallow containers, or smaller pots, and stand them in a sink of iced water, stirring now and then, or use a blast chiller if there is one. As soon as it has cooled, within the time the Centre's food safety plan gives, I cover it, label it with the name and the date, and store it in the fridge at 5 °C or below, or freeze it at -18 °C or below. I use it within the time the plan allows, oldest first. To reheat, I take only what I need, heat it in a pan, stirring, and bring soups and stocks to the boil, so the core reaches at least about 74 °C, checked with a clean probe. I reheat it once only. Then I hold it at about 63 °C or above in a bain-marie, and throw away any reheated food that is left.
markingPoints: Explains the danger zone and why large pots are a risk
Cool quickly: shallow containers, ice bath, stirring (or blast chiller)
Cover, label, date; refrigerate at 5 °C or below or freeze at -18 °C or below
Reheat to the boil or at least about 74 °C core, checked; once only
Hot-hold at about 63 °C or above; throw away reheated leftovers

essays.stem: Compare clear soups and thick soups. Give examples of each, including Jamaican soups.
essays.modelAnswer: Clear soups are thin and are not thickened. They are based on a good, clear stock. Some are broths, which have pieces of meat and vegetables in them, such as chicken broth or a clear vegetable soup. The finest clear soup is consommé, a very clear, strong soup made by clarifying stock with a 'raft' of minced lean meat, egg white and vegetables, which rises to the top and traps the cloudiness. Clear soups are often served as a light starter. Thick soups are thickened in some way. Purée soups are thickened by blending the cooked vegetables or pulses in them, such as pumpkin soup or split pea soup. Cream soups have cream or milk added, such as cream of callaloo. Velouté soups are thickened with a roux. Chowders are thick fish or seafood soups, often with potato. Most Jamaican soups are thick and hearty, served as a full meal: red peas soup is thickened by the peas and yam; pepperpot soup by callaloo, okra and coconut milk; and chicken soup and fish tea have pumpkin, ground provisions and dumplings in them.
markingPoints: Clear soups are not thickened and are based on a clear stock
Examples of clear soups: broth, consommé (clarified with a raft)
Thick soups are thickened: purée, cream, velouté, chowder
Correct examples of thick soups
Jamaican soups classed correctly as thick, with how each is thickened

practical1.title: Stocks and sauces: chicken stock, fish stock, béchamel with cheese sauce, and tomato sauce
practical1.brief: As a group, make a white chicken stock, a fish stock, a béchamel sauce with a cheese (Mornay) sauce from it, and a tomato sauce. The stock is started first. Two members prepare and blanch the chicken bones, start the stock and skim it through the session, and one prepares the fish bones and makes the fish stock, simmering it for about 20 minutes only. Each member, in turn, makes a roux and adds milk to make part of the béchamel, with the assessor watching, so every member shows the method. Then the group makes the cheese sauce and the tomato sauce. Every member tastes with a clean spoon, checks the consistency, strains one of the items, and helps to cool the stocks in an ice bath and label them. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the sauces are done, the stocks are chilled and the area is clean.
materials: About 2 kg raw chicken bones and 1 kg white fish bones and heads (gills removed)
Onion, carrot, celery, leek if available, thyme, bay leaf, parsley stalks, peppercorns
Butter, plain flour, milk, cheese, an onion and clove for the béchamel
Tomatoes or tinned tomatoes, garlic, tomato paste
Stockpot, heavy saucepans, wooden spoons, whisks, ladles, skimmer
Fine strainer or chinois, muslin, measuring jugs and scales
Shallow containers, ice, labels, probe thermometer
photos: The bones blanched and the mirepoix and bouquet garni prepared
The chicken stock simmering, being skimmed
Each member's roux, and the milk being added
The béchamel coating the back of a spoon, and the finished cheese sauce
The tomato sauce, and the fish stock being strained
The stocks cooling in an ice bath, then labelled in the fridge
The work area cleaned at the end
checklist: Started the stock with cold water and skimmed it, with no hard boiling and no salt
Simmered the fish stock for about 20 minutes only
Made a roux of the right colour without burning it
Added the milk gradually and stirred to give a smooth, lump-free sauce

practical2.title: Jamaican red peas soup with spinners, pepperpot soup, and cream of pumpkin soup
practical2.brief: As a group, make three soups, 6 portions of each: red peas soup with spinners, pepperpot soup, and cream of pumpkin soup. Use red peas that the Centre soaked overnight, with the soaking water thrown away, and boil them hard in fresh water before simmering (or use a pressure cooker as the maker says). Two members lead the red peas soup, two lead the pepperpot soup (callaloo, okra, coconut milk and ground provisions), and one leads the pumpkin soup; each member also helps with the others. Every member rolls spinners for the red peas soup, prepares part of the vegetables, and takes a turn to skim, taste with a clean spoon and season. The pumpkin soup is blended safely, with the assessor watching. Each member checks and records the temperature of one soup with a clean probe before it is served, and the group serves one bowl of each soup with a garnish. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the bowls are served and the area is clean.

Flour and salt for spinners and dumplings
Thyme, scallion, garlic, pimento berries, whole Scotch bonnet peppers
Large pots or a pressure cooker, ladles, skimmer, blender or stick blender
